title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 4: Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council
keywords: Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council
the full-time vanguards of the judiciary
primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3) -- CJP's September 16, 2007 Inquirer column answering critics who would abolish the JBC and revert to Commission-on-Appointments confirmation, arguing instead to 'strengthen the anti-political shield of the judiciary, not... shove it back to the partisan mud'

His structural proposal: empower the Supreme Court to appoint the three regular JBC members (from the retired justices, the IBP and the legal academe) and let the President name only the private-sector representative without CA confirmation -- giving the Court four seats, the President two and Congress two, to depoliticize selection

The global context: the JBC, created 20 years earlier, reflects a worldwide reform adopted in 25-plus countries (per Judge Sandra Oxner's study), where such councils -- much larger abroad -- variously nominate or even appoint judges, with the chief justice usually chairing (and Japan letting the Supreme Court do the work)

The JBC's past process reforms (its 2000 Rules, the Pimentel single-member integrity veto, full-time members and staff, media-opened interviews, and the JBC website) and CJP's further 'humble suggestions' -- public votes, a judges'-style ethics code, and full-time members held to the 'proven competence, integrity, probity and independence' standard
sub_topics: The critics' proposal and CJP's reply: because of the JBC's structural deficiencies, some would abolish it and restore CA confirmation, but CJP argues that the regular JBC members (who need CA confirmation and may seek reappointment) are themselves 'vulnerable to the same political pressures,' so the answer is to 'strengthen the anti-political shield,' not return to 'the partisan mud'

The structural fix: empower the Supreme Court to appoint the three regular members representing the retired justices, the Integrated Bar and the legal academe, while the President names only the private-sector representative (no CA confirmation) -- yielding two presidential seats, two congressional, and four for the Court, to 'further depoliticize' the process

The global trend: the JBC (created 20 years earlier) is part of a worldwide reform adopted 'in one form or another, in more than 25 countries,' especially in Europe and Latin America, 'heralded as a way of depoliticizing appointments, guaranteeing the selection of better judges, and advancing judicial independence'

Comparative models (per Judge Sandra Oxner of the Commonwealth Judicial Institute of Canada): councils abroad average about 20 members; in France and Italy they actually appoint (chaired by the head of state), more often the chief justice chairs, and in Japan 'the Supreme Court performs the work of the council'

Past process reforms: with systemic change requiring constitutional amendment, the JBC began in 1988 without rules or staff (regular members part-time), then promulgated the 'Rules of the Judicial and Bar Council' on October 10, 2000 to implement the 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence' standard -- amended, at Senator Aquilino Pimentel Jr.'s instance, to let a single member veto an applicant of 'questionable integrity'

Professionalizing the Council: it later required full-time service and regular compensation of the four regular members, and in late 2005 hired a full-time staff under an executive officer to verify candidates' 'reputation for honesty, incorruptibility, irreproachable conduct'

Transparency steps: the JBC opened candidate interviews to the media (while refusing 'legislative-type investigations' that would diminish judges' dignity), and CJP launched the JBC website (jbc.supremecourt.gov.ph) on April 21, 2006

CJP's 'humble suggestions': (1) make public the names of JBC members voting for listed candidates, as justices' votes are known; (2) have regular members observe the judges' code of ethics by analogy (e.g., avoid socializing with candidates); and (3) hold the full-time regular members to the same 'proven competence, integrity, probity and independence' demanded of judges

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's September 16, 2007 Inquirer column, answers critics who would abolish the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) and revert to Commission-on-Appointments confirmation. He resists: the regular JBC members, who need CA confirmation and may seek reappointment, are themselves 'vulnerable to the same political pressures,' and judges as presidential appointees still feel executive influence -- so the answer is to 'strengthen the anti-political shield of the judiciary, not... shove it back to the partisan mud.' His structural proposal: let the Supreme Court appoint the three regular members representing the retired justices, the Integrated Bar and the legal academe, while the President names only the private-sector representative without CA confirmation -- giving the Court four seats to the President's and Congress's two each, to 'further depoliticize' selection. He sets this in global context: the JBC, then 20 years old, reflects a worldwide reform adopted 'in more than 25 countries,' and, citing Judge Sandra Oxner's study, notes councils abroad average about 20 members, actually appoint judges in France and Italy, are usually chaired by the chief justice, and in Japan are simply done by the Supreme Court. Because systemic change needs a constitutional amendment, he reviews the JBC's interim process reforms -- its October 10, 2000 Rules (implementing 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' amended at Senator Pimentel's instance to allow a single-member veto for 'questionable integrity'), full-time members and staff (from late 2005), media-opened interviews, and the JBC website he launched on April 21, 2006. He closes with three 'humble suggestions': make public the votes of JBC members for listed candidates (as justices' votes are known), have regular members observe the judges' code of ethics by analogy (no socializing with candidates), and hold those full-time members to the same 'proven competence, integrity, probity and independence' demanded of judges.
